newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan MPs attack Israel on settlements, Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: Jordan MPs attack Israel on settlements, Jerusalem.

text.p: Jordanian parliamentarians on Tuesday condemned Israeli actions in Arab East Jerusalem and the rest of the West Bank as a danger to the kingdom's security amid calls by Islamists for Amman to break ties with Israel.
It came during a rare special session to debate Israel's Jewish housing plans in Arab East Jerusalem and its settlement policy in Palestinian territories.
Deputies in the 80 seat-chamber voted last Sunday in favour of an Islamist motion to convene the session in face of government opposition.

Former Prime Minister Taher al-Masri told parliament that the government should freeze normalisation ties with Israel and announce a "review of what has so far been agreed between the two states" since ending a four-decade state of war in 1994.
"What pressure does Israel feel when Israeli officials repeatedly come to Amman and find a welcoming and warm atmosphere ... what (official) position is this?" said Masri, a liberal independent MP.
His comments, echoing widespread criticism of a "weak" Jordanian attitude towards Israel, came as King Hussein was hosting a lunch for Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai.
A chorus of deputies attacked Israel for violating its peace treaty with Jordan, especially over a clause on Moslem sites in Jerusalem which safeguarded Jordan's special role.

Even pro-government deputies called for brakes on ties and linking progress in relations with ending Jewish settlement in Arab land. Some independent deputies joined Islamist calls for ending ties with Israel.

Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti agreed with deputies that ... "Israeli actions were fuelling tension that threatens the peace process and opens the door to possibilities the Israelis themselves would not be able to contain or even imagine their extent or content."

However Kabariti, while saying Israel had breached part of its peace treaty with Jordan which recognised Jordan's "special role" in Jerusalem, said it would be self-defeating to sever ties and leave Palestinians more vulnerable to Israel.
"What would it mean to turn our backs on the peace process ... but to let down our brother Palestinians and leaving them to become prey to the Israeli ogre," Kabariti said.

Kabariti however assured deputies that Israel could not expect ... "to build normal ties with Jordan as long as it continued its settlement policy in Jerusalem," warning that peace could not go on indefinitely with Jewish settlement building.
The mood in the chamber reflects growing popular frustration with Israel and adds to widespread disenchantment with the few tangible benefits of peace with Israel.
Many of Jordan's 4.2 million people are Palestinians with strong family ties across the Jordan River and officials fear domestic repercussions if violence erupts in Palestinian areas.
The kingdom has absorbed successive waves of Palestinian refugees since Israel's creation in 1948.
